Every other unit gives you words; this one gives you a method for producing words you were never taught, and for reading words you have never seen. English builds meaning out of parts, and once you can see the parts, a large vocabulary stops being something you memorise and starts being something you assemble.

visual.lectureScript:
This unit is different from the others, because it is not about a structure. It is about a method.
English has an enormous vocabulary and most of it is built rather than invented. Once you can see how a word is assembled, three things happen: you can guess the meaning of words you have never met, you can produce words nobody taught you, and your reading speed goes up considerably, because you stop stopping.
First pattern: the negative prefixes.
Un-, dis-, in-, and the forms of in- that change shape.
The honest position first. There is no rule that reliably tells you which prefix a given word takes. Unhappy, dishonest, incorrect — they are learned. But there are two strong tendencies and one rule that is completely predictable, and together they cover a great deal.
Tendency one: words of Germanic origin — the short, ordinary ones — tend to take un-. Unhappy, unkind, unfair, unable, unusual.
Tendency two: words that came into English from Latin, usually longer and more formal, tend to take in-. Incorrect, incomplete, inaccurate, invisible.
Dis- is a third group and it often attaches to verbs. Disagree, disappear, dislike, disconnect. It also does adjectives — dishonest, dissimilar.
Now the rule that is completely predictable, and this is the useful part.
In- changes its shape to match the letter that follows it.
Before l, it becomes il-. Illegal, illogical, illiterate.
Before r, it becomes ir-. Irregular, irrelevant, irresponsible.
Before m or p, it becomes im-. Impossible, impatient, immature, improper.
Everywhere else it stays in-. Incorrect, inaccurate, invisible.
That is not a tendency. It is mechanical, it has almost no exceptions, and it means you never have to wonder whether it is inlegal or illegal.
And two warnings. Some words take a prefix you would not expect — unable rather than inable, though the noun is inability. And some in- words are not negatives at all: invaluable does not mean not valuable, it means extremely valuable. Inflammable does not mean fireproof — it means it burns. That second one matters in the real world.
Second pattern: the adjective suffixes.
-able and -ible both mean can be done or tending to.
The useful fact: -able is much more common, and it is the one still producing new words. If you are guessing, guess -able. Readable, workable, adaptable, manageable.
-ible tends to appear on Latin roots that do not stand alone as English words. Visible, possible, terrible, edible — notice vis, poss, terr, ed are not English words. That is the pattern, and it works most of the time.
Compare: readable comes from read, which is a word. Visible comes from vis, which is not.
-ous means having the quality of. Dangerous, ambitious, cautious, generous, hazardous.
And the spelling rule that catches everybody: when a word ends in a silent e, you usually drop it before -able. Value becomes valuable. Desire becomes desirable. But you keep it after a soft c or g, to protect the sound. Notice becomes noticeable. Manage becomes manageable. If you dropped the e there you would get noticable, which would be pronounced with a hard c.
Third pattern: compound nouns, and the question everybody asks — one word, two words, or a hyphen?
The honest answer is that English is inconsistent and moving. Compounds usually start as two words, acquire a hyphen as they become familiar, and end up as one word. Data base became data-base became database. Web site became website. It is happening now with several words, which is why you will see them written both ways by careful writers.
So there is no rule, and here is what to do instead. Check a current dictionary for the specific word. And be consistent within one document, which matters more than being right.
There is one thing worth knowing about how compounds mean. The second word is the thing; the first word describes it. A workload is a load. A workforce is a force. A database is a base. Read the second word first and the compound usually explains itself.
And stress, which is how you tell a compound from an ordinary phrase in speech. A greenhouse — stress on green — is a building for plants. A green house — even stress — is a house that is green. Compounds take the stress on the first part. That distinction is invisible in writing and completely clear in speech.
Fourth pattern: abstract nouns.
These are nouns for qualities and ideas rather than things you can point at. Efficiency, reliability, awareness, responsibility.
The suffixes that build them: -ness from adjectives, -ity from adjectives, -ment from verbs, -tion from verbs, -ance and -ence from verbs.
Happy becomes happiness. Reliable becomes reliability. Arrange becomes arrangement. Inform becomes information. Perform becomes performance.
And here is the thing worth knowing about them, which is a warning rather than a rule.
Abstract nouns let you avoid saying who did something. There was a failure of communication. Compare: nobody told the warehouse. The first has no person in it at all, and that is often exactly why it was chosen.
This is called nominalisation, and official writing runs on it. The implementation of the recommendation is under consideration. Somebody is thinking about whether to do it.
So abstract nouns are genuinely useful for talking about ideas, and they are also the main tool for writing sentences where nothing happens and nobody is responsible. Knowing how they are built lets you take them apart, which is a reading skill as much as a writing one.
Go to Patterns.

readings.title: The One Rule That Is Actually Mechanical
readings.passageScript:
Most of English spelling is history rather than logic, and most prefix choices have to be learned. Unhappy but incorrect but dishonest — there is no test that tells you which.
There are two tendencies worth knowing. Short, ordinary words of Germanic origin tend to take un-: unkind, unfair, unable, unusual. Longer, more formal words that came from Latin tend to take in-: incorrect, incomplete, inaccurate, invisible.
Those are tendencies. They will fail sometimes.
But there is one rule inside this area that is completely mechanical, and it is worth ten minutes because it never lets you down.
When in- meets certain letters, it changes shape to match them.
Before l it becomes il-. Illegal, illogical, illiterate, illegible.
Before r it becomes ir-. Irregular, irrelevant, irresponsible, irreversible.
Before m or p it becomes im-. Impossible, impatient, immature, improper, immoral.
Everywhere else it stays in-. Incorrect, inaccurate, invisible, incomplete.
That is not a tendency and it has almost no exceptions. You will never need to wonder whether it is inlegal or illegal, because inlegal is not something English can produce.
The reason is pronunciation. Try saying inlegal and inregular quickly. Your mouth wants to change the n, and centuries ago it did.
Two warnings before you use this.
Some words take the prefix you would not expect. Unable rather than inable — but the noun is inability, with in-. English is not consistent even with itself.
And some in- words are not negatives at all. Invaluable does not mean not valuable; it means so valuable it cannot be measured. Inflammable does not mean fireproof; it means it catches fire easily. That second one has caused real accidents, which is why safety labelling now uses flammable instead.

readings.title: Sentences With Nobody In Them
readings.passageScript:
Abstract nouns name qualities and ideas — efficiency, reliability, awareness, responsibility. They are genuinely useful, because you cannot discuss ideas without them.
They are also the main tool English has for writing sentences in which nothing happens and nobody is responsible.
Compare these.
Nobody told the warehouse.
There was a failure of communication.
The two describe the same event. The first has a person in it — or rather, a missing person, which is the point. The second has no people at all. Failure and communication are both abstract nouns, and between them they have absorbed the entire question of who should have said something.
This is called nominalisation: turning a verb into a noun. Communicate becomes communication. Implement becomes implementation. Decide becomes decision. Fail becomes failure.
Official and corporate writing runs on it, and once you can see it you will see it everywhere.
The implementation of the recommendation is under consideration. Somebody is thinking about whether to do it.
There has been a reduction in staffing levels. They cut jobs.
An error occurred during the processing of your application. We made a mistake.
Mistakes were made. Notice this one has no agent even in the verb.
The unpacking method is simple and it works nearly every time. Find the abstract noun, turn it back into a verb, and then ask the question the sentence has avoided: who did it?
There was a failure of communication. Fail to communicate. Who failed to communicate with whom?
Often the answer is not in the document at all, and that absence is the information.
This is a reading skill first. It is also a writing decision — sometimes you genuinely want to describe a process rather than blame a person, and nominalisation is the correct tool for that. The problem is not the grammar. It is using it without noticing, and finding that your own writing has quietly stopped saying who does what.

  operations.

  and a proactive approach to problem
  identification and resolution.

  Responsibilities include the co-
  ordination of inbound deliveries, the
  maintenance of stock accuracy, and the
  provision of support to the wider
  workforce.

  Experience of workload prioritisation
  in a high-turnover environment is
  desirable but not essential.

  optimisation of operations
     making things work better

  problem identification and resolution
     spotting problems and fixing them

  co-ordination of inbound deliveries
     booking in deliveries

  maintenance of stock accuracy
     counting the stock and keeping the
     numbers right

grammar.title: Negative prefixes
grammar.explanation: Two tendencies for guessing, and one rule that is completely mechanical. The mechanical part is the useful part.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
TWO TENDENCIES (they can fail)
  Germanic, short, ordinary  -> UN-
     unkind, unfair, unable, unusual
  Latin, longer, formal      -> IN-
     incorrect, incomplete, inaccurate
  DIS- often on verbs
     disagree, disappear, disconnect

THE MECHANICAL RULE - no exceptions
  IN- changes shape to match what follows

  before L -> IL-
     illegal, illogical, illiterate
  before R -> IR-
     irregular, irrelevant, irresponsible
  before M or P -> IM-
     impossible, impatient, immature
  everywhere else -> IN-
     incorrect, inaccurate, invisible

  "inlegal" is not something English
  can produce.

TWO WARNINGS
  unable, but the noun is INability.
  Some in- words are NOT negatives:
     invaluable  = extremely valuable
     inflammable = it BURNS
  ^ this one has caused real accidents.
grammar.workedExample:
You want the negative of legal.
1. Legal is Latin-origin, so the tendency says in-.
2. Now apply the mechanical rule. What letter does legal start with? L.
3. Before l, in- becomes il-.
4. Result: illegal.
Now relevant.
1. Latin-origin, so in-.
2. It starts with r, so in- becomes ir-.
3. Result: irrelevant. Note the double r — the prefix ends in r and the word begins with r, and both are kept.
Now patient.
1. Latin-origin, so in-.
2. It starts with p, so in- becomes im-.
3. Result: impatient.
And one where the tendency does the work instead. Kind is short and ordinary, so un-: unkind. The mechanical rule does not apply because there is no in- involved.
grammar.commonMistake: Producing inlegal or inregular, which the assimilation rule rules out entirely. The other error is assuming every in- word is a negative — invaluable means extremely valuable, and inflammable means it burns. And forgetting the double letter in irrelevant, irregular, immature and illegible, where the prefix and the root each keep their letter.
grammar.memoryTip: Before l, r, m or p, in- changes to match. Everywhere else it stays in-.

grammar.answerKey:
1. illegal  2. irregular  3. impatient  4. incorrect  5. unkind  6. dishonest  7. illogical  8. irrelevant  9. impossible  10. inaccurate  11. unable  12. immature
The assimilation rule produced 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 9 and 12 — every one where in- met l, r, m or p.
Numbers 1, 2, 7, 8 and 12 all have double letters, because the prefix keeps its letter and so does the root: il+legal, ir+regular, im+mature.
Number 11 is the exception the card warns about: unable, not inable — though the noun is inability.

grammar.title: Adjective suffixes
grammar.explanation: Three suffixes that build adjectives, one reliable guessing strategy, and a spelling rule that catches almost everybody.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
-ABLE and -IBLE both mean
  "can be done" or "tending to"

WHICH ONE? A USABLE TEST
  -ABLE is far more common and it is the
  one still producing new words.
  If guessing, guess -ABLE.

  -ABLE attaches to real English words
     read -> readable
     work -> workable
     adapt -> adaptable

  -IBLE attaches to Latin roots that
  are NOT English words on their own
     vis  -> visible
     poss -> possible
     terr -> terrible
     flex -> flexible

-OUS = "having the quality of"
  dangerous, ambitious, cautious,
  hazardous, generous

THE SILENT E RULE
  usually DROP the e before -able
     value  -> valuable
     desire -> desirable
  but KEEP it after soft c or g
     notice -> noticeable
     manage -> manageable
  ^ dropping it would harden the sound:
    "noticable" would have a hard c.
grammar.workedExample:
You want the adjective from value, meaning worth a lot.
1. Choose the suffix. Value is an ordinary English word, so -able.
2. Now the spelling. Value ends in a silent e.
3. Is the letter before the e a soft c or g? No, it is u.
4. So drop the e: valuable.
Now notice, meaning able to be noticed.
1. Notice is an English word, so -able.
2. It ends in a silent e.
3. Is the letter before the e a soft c or g? Yes — c, pronounced as an s.
4. So keep the e: noticeable.
5. Check why: without the e you would have noticable, and the c would harden to a k sound. The e is protecting the pronunciation.
And one -ible. Take flex. Is flex an ordinary English word standing alone? Not really — it is a Latin root. So -ible: flexible.
grammar.commonMistake: Dropping the e after a soft c or g — noticable, managable, changable. All three are wrong and all three would change how the word sounds. The other error is over-applying the -ible pattern; if the root is a real English word, it takes -able almost every time, and -able is the safer guess when you are unsure.
grammar.memoryTip: Real word takes -able. Latin root takes -ible. Keep the e after soft c or g.

12. caution
grammar.answerKey:
1. valuable  2. noticeable  3. manageable  4. desirable  5. readable  6. visible  7. flexible  8. hazardous  9. ambitious  10. adaptable  11. changeable  12. cautious
The e was kept in 2, 3 and 11 — noticeable, manageable, changeable — because each has a soft c or g before it. Dropping it would harden the sound.
The e was dropped in 1 and 4, where the preceding letter is not c or g.
Numbers 6 and 7 take -ible because vis and flex are Latin roots rather than English words. Numbers 5 and 10 take -able because read and adapt are ordinary words.

grammar.title: Compound nouns
grammar.explanation: One word, two words or a hyphen — English is inconsistent and changing, so there is no rule. What there is instead is a way of reading them and a way of hearing them.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
ONE WORD, TWO, OR HYPHENATED?
  There is no reliable rule.

  Compounds MOVE over time:
     data base -> data-base -> database
     web site  -> website
  Several are moving right now, which is
  why careful writers disagree.

  WHAT TO DO:
   1 check a current dictionary
   2 be CONSISTENT within one document
     (this matters more than being right)

HOW TO READ ONE
  the SECOND word is the thing.
  the FIRST word describes it.

     a workload  is a LOAD
     a workforce is a FORCE
     a database  is a BASE
     a timescale is a SCALE

  Read the second word first and the
  compound usually explains itself.

HOW TO HEAR ONE - STRESS
  compound -> stress on the FIRST part

     a GREENhouse = a building for plants
     a green HOUSE = a house that is green

  Invisible in writing.
  Completely clear in speech.
grammar.workedExample:
You meet the word timescale for the first time.
1. Split it: time and scale.
2. The second word is the thing, so this is a kind of scale.
3. The first word describes it: a scale of time.
4. So it means the period over which something happens. You have worked it out without a dictionary.
Now the spoken version. Somebody says they are going to the greenhouse.
1. Listen to the stress. If it is on green, it is a compound — the building for plants.
2. If both words are evenly stressed, it is an ordinary phrase — a house that happens to be green.
That distinction cannot be written down and it is completely reliable in speech, which is why compounds are easier to identify when heard than when read.
And the writing decision: is it timescale, time-scale or time scale? Check a dictionary, then use the same form throughout your document. Consistency is what a reader notices; the specific choice is not.
grammar.commonMistake: Trying to derive the one-word-or-two question from a rule. There is not one, English is actively changing, and time spent looking for it is wasted. The other error is reading a compound by its first word — assuming a workforce is about work in general rather than being a kind of force. The second element is the head of the compound and it carries the category.
grammar.memoryTip: Second word is the thing. Stress on the first part means a compound.
grammar.practice:
Say what each compound is, using the second-word rule.
1. workload
2. workforce
3. database
4. timescale
5. feedback
6. turnover
7. Now say what the stress difference is between a greenhouse and a green house.
grammar.answerKey:
1. A load — of work.
2. A force — of workers.
3. A base — of data.
4. A scale — of time.
5. Back — information fed back. (This one is less transparent than the others, which happens as compounds age.)
6. Over — from turning over. (Also opaque, and it means two different things: staff leaving, and total sales.)
7. A GREENhouse has the stress on green and is a building for plants. A green HOUSE has even stress and is a house that is green.
Numbers 1 to 4 are transparent — the parts explain the whole. Numbers 5 and 6 are not, and that is the normal fate of a compound as it becomes common: the parts stop being visible.
That is worth knowing, because it tells you when to stop trying to analyse and simply learn the word.

grammar.title: Abstract nouns and unpacking them
grammar.explanation: Nouns for qualities and ideas. Useful for discussing concepts, and the main tool English has for writing sentences in which nobody is responsible.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
BUILDING THEM
  -NESS  from adjectives
     aware -> awareness
  -ITY   from adjectives
     reliable -> reliability
     flexible -> flexibility
  -MENT  from verbs
     arrange -> arrangement
  -TION  from verbs
     inform -> information
  -ANCE / -ENCE from verbs
     perform -> performance

NOMINALISATION - the warning
  turning a verb into a noun removes
  the person doing it.

  "Nobody told the warehouse."
  "There was a failure of communication."
  ^ same event. Second has NO PEOPLE.

OFFICIAL WRITING RUNS ON THIS
  "The implementation of the
   recommendation is under consideration."
     = somebody is thinking about
       whether to do it.

UNPACKING - three steps
   1 find the abstract noun
   2 turn it back into a verb
   3 ask: WHO did it?

  Often the answer is not in the document.
  That absence is the information.
grammar.workedExample:
You read: there has been a reduction in staffing levels.
1. Find the abstract noun. Reduction.
2. Turn it back into a verb. Reduce.
3. Ask who did it. Who reduced the staffing levels?
4. The sentence does not say. That is not an accident — reduction was chosen precisely because it does not require a subject.
5. The plain version: they cut jobs.
Now a second one: an error occurred during the processing of your application.
1. Abstract nouns: error, processing.
2. Verbs: err, process.
3. Who? Somebody processed the application and somebody made the mistake, and the sentence names neither. Occurred is doing extra work here — it makes the error sound like weather.
4. Plain version: we made a mistake.
The method is the same every time, and the third step is the one that produces the finding. Often the answer is simply absent, and noticing the absence is the whole skill.
grammar.commonMistake: Using nominalisation without noticing, which is how writing quietly stops saying who does what. It is not an error of grammar — sometimes you genuinely want to describe a process rather than name a person, and the abstract noun is the right tool. The problem is reaching for it by default, so that your own writing becomes vaguer than you intended.
grammar.memoryTip: Find the noun, make it a verb, ask who did it.
grammar.practice:
Unpack each sentence into plain English with a person in it.
1. There was a failure of communication.
2. The implementation of the recommendation is under consideration.
3. There has been a reduction in staffing levels.
4. An error occurred during the processing of your application.
5. Responsibility for the delay has not been established.
6. The optimisation of warehouse operations is a key priority.
grammar.answerKey:
1. Nobody told the warehouse. (fail to communicate — who failed?)
2. Somebody is thinking about whether to do it. (implement, recommend, consider — three verbs, no people)
3. They cut jobs. (reduce — who reduced?)
4. We made a mistake. (err, process — occurred makes it sound like weather)
5. Nobody has worked out whose fault the delay was. (be responsible, establish — two agents missing)
6. We want the warehouse to work better. (optimise, prioritise — and note that key priority says nothing about how key)
In every one, at least one person is missing from the original. In numbers 2 and 6 the plain version had to invent a subject, because the original genuinely does not contain one.
Number 4 is worth a second look. Occurred is not a nominalisation, but it does the same job — it makes something that somebody did sound like something that happened.

answerKey.reviewStatus: AI-assisted authoring — pending curriculum reviewer sign-off

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: valuable — The silent e is dropped before -able, because the preceding letter is u rather than a soft c or g.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: -able — It is far more common and it is the form still producing new words. -ible tends to attach to Latin roots that do not stand alone as English words.
answerKey.reviewStatus: AI-assisted authoring — pending curriculum reviewer sign-off

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Force — In a compound noun the second word is the thing and the first describes it. Read the second word first and most compounds explain themselves.
answerKey.reviewStatus: AI-assisted authoring — pending curriculum reviewer sign-off

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: By the stress — a compound stresses the first part — GREENhouse is a building for plants; green HOUSE is a house that is green. The distinction is invisible in writing and completely reliable in speech.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Check a dictionary, then be consistent — English is inconsistent and actively changing here — compounds move from two words to hyphenated to one over time. Consistency within a document matters more than the specific choice.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Turning a verb into a noun — Communicate becomes communication, decide becomes decision. It is useful for discussing ideas and it is also the main tool for writing sentences with nobody in them.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: The people — Nobody told the warehouse describes the same event and contains a person. Failure and communication between them absorb the question of who should have spoken.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Find the noun, make it a verb, ask who did it — The third step produces the finding. Often the answer is not in the document at all, and that absence is the information.
